Given that you are a primary care physician, you may or may not feel comfortable speaking about the psychological causes of trans-genderism (not sure if that is a word) but have you noticed whether there are biological causes?

Transgenderism or transsexualism most certainly has a biological cause, most likely during fetal development. There is a certain sequence of hormonal changes that have to occur in the mother and fetus, and if there is a hiccup in this sequence, neurological development will follow one gender path, while the rest of the body follows another.

MRIs of the brains of transgender women show the same structure as natal women, and PET scans show that certain stimuli (such as colors) set off a gender-based neurological reaction.

There's no lab test or radiology that's going to identify a transsexual person. It is self-reported. That said, however, someone who is wanting to undergo SRS will generally live full-time as their desired gender for a year or more, and also undergo extensive counseling, before they schedule surgery. And a surgeon will never do that surgery without a letter from a therapist specializing in gender disorders saying that the patient fits the criteria for SRS. Therapists in the field are familiar with the pathologies that might confuse a non-transgender person.The chances of someone changing their mind after surgery is low, though it has happened.

My role is not to certify them mentally, but physically, that they can undergo the procedure. If someone has physical problems that make them a high risk, I'll notify the surgeon.

Also, note that SRS isn't the desired outcome for everyone. Some people are perfectly happy with hormone therapy and a name change. Transgender men rarely get bottom surgery, though they may get mastectomy. Nor is FFS necessary, either. Most of the transgender women I know look perfectly fine with some makeup and TLC.

That said, there are tremendous psychological pressures that develop in the person, beginning in childhood and becoming more prominent during adolescence. This, combined with societal response to gender-inappropriate behaviors can create a lot of psychological problems. These lead to much higher rates of depression, suicide and drug use, both before and after the condition is recognized and support programs are in place.
